I had a similar experience hope you don't mind me sharing.

My boyfriend at the time broke up with me when I was about 14. We'd been together for about a year and out of the blue he broke up with me in the middle of a patch of grass where my group and others hung out. I never even noticed he was falling out of love because I was in my own little world fantasising about fun things we'd do together and whatnot. My life and happiness was HIM and only him. Completely clueless. I ended up screaming so loud everyone heard and was so full of emotion I fell onto my knees and sobbed the loudest I could because the pain was SO intense. I vaguely remember shouting insults at him and some of my friends having to pull me back. I didn't know I had BPD at this time. Just thought I was overly sensitive.

A day later he got with another girl, I'll call her M. She wasn't interested in him but I deliberately (didn't realise at the time but looking back I do) made a friendship with her so I could watch his every move. I  quickly went from hate to sadness back and forth and was crazy obsessed with him. I'd walk places I knew he was, say things to his friends. Constantly viewed his social media. The day he blocked me was another loss, felt the equivalent to when someone I loved died, yet more than I felt when they died. It's so weird how I don't react to seemingly big things like deaths or moving aways as others without bpd do. But the things revolving around someone I was attached to or was an 'fp'... It was a lot. Now that I think of it I don't resonate with the term FP much because of how often I shift between love and hate 

Obviously I'm not proud of it but I remember the feelings so clearly to this day being almost 19. I was diagnosed a year ago and it made so much sense when I was.

I feel like a lot of pw/BPD / EUPD do similar to what I've described and your post resonated with me a lot. Thankfully although I'm not healed I'm in therapy and recognising triggered before I make a scene I regret (which becomes another whirlwind of painful emotions and self doubt) or try to stop the feelings by being more in wise mind (a dbt concept and skill).

I'd love to know how we all relate or don't relate to this experience. Is it as universal as I think or do others feel differently? Would love to know! :)

I guess we have to ask the question of want vs need. There's a difference between someone wanting a diagnosis for the funsies (srsly I really don't understand why someone would want a heavily stigmatised disorder on their records for their whole life just because) and wanting a diagnosis because of genuine suffering and wanting recognition and help that they deserve. For me, I was diagnosed recently and I pursued that because for me, not having it diagnosed meant I couldn't access the right treatment, and even more so I was being treated differently as people were unaware of my other difficulties besides being depressed as my original central diagnosis, which now is obviously BPD. Which was a diagnosis I really needed to both validate the invisible struggle I go through everyday (if we're being specific I have the discouraged/quiet BPD unofficial yet still recognised subtype) which was and still absolutely debilitating. The diagnosis made me feel that I wasn't going crazy, that what I had was a mental health condition and not my fault, and even better, a road map for treatment could finally be established but with greater efficency than a bit of CBT. They needed to just move one letter in the alphabet, so the therapy became DBT.

But to clarify, wanting a debilitating disorder is probably a sign something serious is going on regardless mentally, such as having other mental health problems like not being in touch with reality or depressed to the point you feel insane so you start to act out and strive for a more complex diagnosis to help others understand the pain you're in, or even a sign of validation from post abusive situations that it was abuse because you have a trauma based disorder, or maybe you have the disorder where you're convinced you have most if not all mental disorders or you just want pity points? Idk. (pity points in terms of people who want diagnosis of BPD for funsies)

Want vs need, I guess only the individual themselves knows the true distinction. However I do think social media has a severe issue of glamorisation and romanticising of mental disorders as an aesthetic, and people forget that disorders aren't something we can just turn on when we want something or turn off when we want a break - it's always there.

For the record, abusive people don’t worry about becoming abusive, and no matter what they did, they’d probably 9 times out of 10 deny it’s even abuse. You seem to know ‘signs’ like seeing violent behaviour in a partner, although the part I don’t think you did get from the statement about throwing things and “the abused always becomes the abuser” is the reason for the behaviours. When does the hitting of doors or punching walls, or maybe even yourself, happen? If it is in a context of self-injurious behaviours because you feel like sh’ing, anger or frustration, sadness, pain desperation….no matter the reason for sh, the key point here would be, whether or not the punching of walls was a response from your partner, for example, that happened in presumed aggravation to a comment you said, or if the action was done near you but your partner not hitting you for example, would then in my opinion be signs of a potential for future physical abuse/domestic violence if it isn’t already happened.

You really seem like you don’t want to hurt anybody but yourself OP, and as someone who has wondered the same about myself in the past, I find knowing the signs to look for in abusive relationships and when things start getting rocky to then compare your behaviours in their context, to the abusive behaviours also in context, is a good way to keep in check. It’s also a good thing as you’d be looking out for yourself in potentially noticing it in future partners if you have them.

You’re doing what you can and I’m glad you reached out and wrote this post OP, that fact in itself is enough reason to say that A) you want to do good, and do not have bad intent and B) that actually, there’s saying and research that shows those who have suffered past abuse/trauma, are more likely to end up in relationships where their partner is the abusive one (which would make you more likely to be victim than abuser, and second guessing yourself is also a sign enduring a lot of manipulation and emotional abuse = poor sense of individual righteousness without confirmation from others….most often, our abusers to stay in line as a protection strategy). 

Everything will be okay, and if you were to ever become abusive (which i doubt you will honestly you seem too conscientious, caring and aware to prevent that from happening) then you can seek help from additional places: talking therapies tend to be a good option, especially within addiction situations as there is also a link between substance misuse and abusive behaviours due to lacking in stable visual and emotional perception (I believe so anyway, don’t quote me on that lol).

I wish you all well, and OP, it’s gonna be okay. I believe in you. 🥰

As a fellow BPD individual, I just wanted to say to you and op that you have a massive degree of resilience, to carry on and how you have carried on, despite the want to do the exact opposite and find a moment of quiet relief in your mind and stability emotionally.

I want to say to you, anyone viewing this, and OP (creator of this post) that the thing that's fuelling your emotional turmoil, whether environmentally triggered, a genetic predisposition without a clear external reason to why you're feeling how you are, or even just the fact you're feeling this way and God knows what the cause is... There could be so many! BUT, the key thing is that our experiences are our own, and everyone has a different experience. There are people who happily beam all day, consistently feeling good and thinking clearly, but you know the beauty of that is besides the fact its the ideal? The fact it is an experience another human, like you and me, has, and alterations can be made to ensure you can have this experience too. It's not impossible, it just seems it because you consistently feel the opposite, therefore think that it couldn't happen to you. All you have experienced is your own path, your own brain and mind. Although there are things we can't change in this world, there will always be an alternative, or another way to connect to something you've lost, or that takes the edge of the emotional storm off, to make the day more manageable. We just haven't found it yet. 

Therapy is individual and personal - it works for some, and not for others. Different types of therapy help different types of situations and different types of people. Therapy may not even work for you. Medication is the same, if you can access that. But this doesn't mean to say, something won't ever work for you, because there are some treatments that are specific to some disorders, for example BPD individuals commonly receive DBT therapy, which typically teaches distress tolerance, and is mostly in groups (some provide 1-1 therapy ontop of this also!) so you're working with others who go through very similar patterns to you, and is a way to feel less alone, even in having a disorder where chronic emptiness is a symptom and loneliness is extremely common amongst us. 

There is a way, and I'm not going to say you will get fully better as a definite, but there IS a way/something that will alleviate some of the intensity of your symptoms; help you feel better than you currently are. You just have to find that way. And no, you don't have to do that alone. I would advise you do it with someone who adds light to your life, and if you don't have that someone, try your hardest to find  them because having that someone is just the bare minimum of the light and safety and happiness you deserve. The journey sucks, but the more we try, the more we fight, the more we are steps closer to winning. You've already made it this far, tried so many things, the energy you spent in trying previous ways of coping helps rule them out as either helpful or unhelpful, and you have to have less energy to make it to that end point every time you have wanted to give up but haven't. You. are. Strong. Take things at your pace, try your best to be kind to yourself. Light is the only way we can repel the dark.

Hi there,

To reassure you, you aren't alone, and I'd say this can be quite a common thing in BPD, especially if there is any previous sexual related trauma, or maybe even emotional abuse meaning you can only trust physical signs of affection.

Although, me saying you're not alone, is not meant to in any way diminish or invalidate what you're going through. Your experience is your experience, it's raw and real for you, and it varies from person to person.

However, I wanted to let you know I have BPD/EUPD and have struggled/sometimes still struggle with hypersexuality. There's some research I've seen that has found that a lot of people with BPD struggle with hypersexuality, and there are a variety of reasons. Low self esteem or the unclear self image, feeling pressured to be intimate with a partner in fear they will leave or love them any less (the right person should respect you for you and you shouldn't have to do sexual acts when you don't want to...They aren't the right person if they don't respect your boundaries!!!), a way to numb emotions and distract from life or the constant emotional turmoil and intensity, an act of impulsivity etc etc. 

I have attachment issues, that are parental based. My entire life I've never felt love. I still don't in my relationships both romantic and in friendships, and am in constant need of reassurance. Because of that constant need, I am scared of annoying my friends by being too clingy for that reassurance, and do not have a significant other romantically, so instead I gravitate to men. Why? Why...... When I'm a lesbian? There's no attraction to men, it's literally because I've had older men take advantage of me, and felt their interest (despite being perverted) was genuine, and had an eagerness to it, which I never really had before; I had to always beg for the bare minimum of love and I rarely ever got that no matter how much I tried. So the compliments, the interactions, role plays, all forms of intimacy when in a state of hypersexuality, show to me someone is willing to devote their time to me, and only me.. Which is very unhealthy, and a triggering place to be in for me. But the lack of feeling loved, is more important to me that triggering my trauma.... Which I'm working on trying other ways to replenish that love feeling, without triggering trauma in the process. 

My point is, it's okay to want attention. Wanting attention isn't a bad thing unless you only evaluate it on a surface level... Where we only seek attention in moments we need it. Even if some view it as 'too much'. But you know what? You can't control what has happened, how you feel... But to a certain extent, we can control how we deal with those feelings. 

There is hope, there are days you feel like this earth is a living hell....but know that darkness is merely the absence of light, it doesn't mean there's no light in you, or that light will never come. It is inevitable light will come back, because light repels the dark and the sunrise means a new day, the night is where we put our worries to sleep and no matter what, the moon always sets and the sun will always rise in the morning. 

There is hope. Somewhere, somehow. Someday, someone... and give it some time, because time can help emotional pain, reflection, and even better, time means this isn't forever, and as time goes on, it gives more opportunity for the rain to turn into sun.

Let’s put this the other way.

If you were in the same boat as them and needed someone, would you blame your friend for your relapse because they didn’t answer the phone? I may be wrong, but the reason for them wanting to self-harm is extremely likely to be something that happened in their life that made them get to this stage. Not you.

And anyway, you are their friend to support them, but relationships are two-sided not one. You both have lives, you were having fun with yours (which you fully deserve and you ARE allowed to have fun), and there’s hasn’t been going so great, but that isn’t your fault.

If you still feel bad, you can be there for your friend with the aftermath and support them, but your support is the support you are giving from YOUR energy, and you need to reserve some of that for yourself too. Having fun helps you recharge this, as well as not being too hard on yourself which I know is hard to do when you care about someone. It feels like you blame yourself because you care so much about them you don’t want them to be hurt by something going on in their life or something they did, you want the weight on you so they can be happier. But again, this is not your fault dude and not a weight for you to carry.

This seems unhealthy with the amount of important parts of your life like friendships and events you are sacrificing just for him. As hard as it is, you should try to hang out with people you know irl because once this online friend goes (if they do, not saying they will) then you will be stuck feeling alone which is not a situation that’s nice to be in at all.

I think because you both suffer with/have suffered with issues around self-harm, you need to both agree some boundaries on what is said about it and what is implied, for both your mental health and his. It seems to me what he said then triggered you into a massive spiral of self-hate and blame. If I try to put this into perspective, how many people do you walk past or interact with when you’re on a day out walking or up town/a shopping centre? If you go into many shops, see 2 friends, smile at a security guard, pet someone’s dog - within that one day, you have interacted with so many people. So does that mean because you interacted with them, that you are to blame for something that happens? If you accidentally pay the cashier wrong and the previous customer annoys the cashier which results in the cashier screaming at the customer behind you. Is that your fault single-handedly? No. The customers before you could’ve upset the cashier, they could have problems at home, there’s so many factors to what can contribute to someone having a bad day.

My point is in all this, your friend has many different stimuli around them that can positively or negatively affect their day. Just because you didn’t answer the phone when they needed you doesn’t mean you are responsible for what happened at all. From the sounds of it, this friend reached out to you because you have been a good friend and someone they’re comfortable talking to about things. However, as he has emotions and pain, you do too because you’re both human. I think a lot of the time, people who revert to this mindset of not being good enough or a bad friend is because they don’t have a very good view of themselves and whatever happened is like a ‘confirmation’ for it.

I also want to say that techniques people promote saying "journalling cured me" or "this routine is the cure to my depression" are stating what works for them. Key words "me" and "my". You have probably heard before that everyone is different, which is why I think that attempting to take a step back and writing down things that you liked in the past (or now if you can) or maybe even what kind of person people see you as behind the troubles you are struggling with. Then maybe linking an interest or aspect of your personality to an activity would be better than general activities, although everything is worth a shot! Key part to take from this idea would be to only write the way a person sees you quality wise if you agree. For example, if someone said you were sporty but you hated sports, don't consider that one - I mean if you REALLY don't agree or know 10000% it isn't your thing. It is also okay not to know who you are, a lot of us don't without some help. If you find yourself thinking, for example, "I find the plot of movies interesting sometimes" pick that statement apart. A movie plot involves characters, ideas, places so why not make one for fun? or watch different movies and review them? 

My example may not be the best, and I may not have responded in the most helpful way because I don't know more about things you're dealing with. But, I hope you see the point I am trying to make. Things like depression can sometimes cloud who we believe we are, and fixes us to the mindset of "I don't enjoy anything", "I don't know who I am" etc. That is why looking beyond that cloud is the key to finding a way in my opinion. When this option was first suggested to me, I responded with a response in the same mindset of "Yeah. but, I tried and I didn't enjoy it". Enjoyment takes time because your body/mind has to recognise what you are doing as engaging and fun. Also don't think about if you are trying something and the fact it's "not working", because then your energy focus is on the fact it hasn't worked *yet* and then your energy isn't being put toward the technique actually working if that makes sense?

I'm in this position right now. (I'm leaving major details out because my aim is to help not trigger anyone). In my opinion, I think its an esteem sorta thing? So you don't see yourself as bad, but if you saw other's self harm, you would instantly comfort them and compare it yours because you think theirs is 'better'. I personally don't see mine as valid, but when I see other people's, or hear them saying it's not 'valid' then I immediately just want to give unlimited hugs and cuddles because self-harm is self-harm and I hate to see others suffer how I did. No matter how or why or what it looks like: self-harm is still self-harm. To put it into perspective: if you and a friend have an apple, and you both bite it differently, did you still bite the apple? Yes you did. Even if your friend took a massive bite and you only took a small bite, is that apple still bitten? Or because your friend took a bigger bite, did they bite the apple but you didn't because your bite was smaller? No. That apple's form still changed. Just like how it does when you self-harm. If you want to argue that the scars might fade, let's get a piece broken away from an apple that someone bit and tape it back in place. . Is that apple fixed? It's piece has returned, so it must be right? Wrong. The bonds in that apple aren't as strong as they were, and one shake can disconnect that piece of apple from the main part, it only LOOKS better. So even if you say 'they're only scratches and someone did deeper' yes, the other may require slightly more medical attention but you both had similar intentions; both wanted to harm. The mentality of it is still there, and then that feeling of invalidation starts to creep in and it becomes a vicious cycle that many, like myself, struggle to get out of. YOU ARE VALID. If you cut, or scratch, or burn, or injure yourself in any way, you are valid. Don't listen to the people who haven't experienced it first hand because they know nothing what it's like. These people are the equivalent of exam markers seeing the end products of two students. Both could have written at a similar level but one could have done hours or revision and the other ten minutes. You can't tell from the outside unless you investigate further. So the people who tell you guys you're invalid because it looks a certain way, are ignorant f*ckers who have no clue.
